math: Target 15, moves 1–3: 15, 11, 7, 3

strategies.title: Make every round add up to the same total

screens.title: Answer each move
text: Find the round total: smallest move + largest move. Whatever your friend does, you do 'round total minus their move'. Make your first move so that what is left is a multiple of the round total.
math: Moves 1–4, round total 5: friend 1 → you 4, friend 3 → you 2
17 counters: take 2 first (17 = 3 × 5 + 2)

modules.title: Choose, design and critique data displays

chapter.title: Match the display to the data
text: Ask what the display is for. Comparing categories: bar graph or pictograph. Parts of one whole: pie chart. Change over time: line graph. Two groups across the same categories: double bar graph.
math: Pie chart angle = (part ÷ whole) × 360°
Pictograph: number = pictures × the value of one picture

chapter.title: Worked: a misleading bar graph
text: A shop's graph shows sales of 82 in March and 88 in April, with the axis starting at 80.
math: 1. On the page, the March bar is 82 − 80 = 2 units tall. — The axis starts at 80
2. The April bar is 88 − 80 = 8 units tall. — Same reason
3. April LOOKS 4 times as big. — 8 ÷ 2 = 4
4. Really, 88 ÷ 82 ≈ 1.07: about 7% more. — Comparing the true values
5. Fix: start the axis at 0, or mark a clear break and say so.
chapter.tip: Bars must start at 0 to compare fairly by height.

chapter.title: A checklist for a clear, honest display
text: Title that says what the data is (not what to think). Labelled axes with units. A scale with equal steps, from 0 for bars. A key for pictures. The source and the number of people asked.
Watch for 3-D effects, pictures that grow in both directions, and percentages that do not add up.
chapter.tip: A picture twice as tall and twice as wide has 4 times the area. Show 'twice as many' with twice as many pictures.

strategies.title: Ask what the display makes you believe

screens.title: Compare the look with the numbers
text: Look at the display first, and say what it seems to show. Then read the numbers. If the look and the numbers disagree, the display is misleading.
math: Axis from 50: bars of 55 and 70 look like 5 and 20 units, a ratio of 4
True ratio: 70 ÷ 55 ≈ 1.3

strategies.title: Choose by the question you are answering

screens.title: Three questions to choose a display
text: 1. Are the values parts of one whole? Pie chart.
2. Is it about change over time? Line graph.
3. Are you comparing categories (or two groups across categories)? Bar graph (or double bar graph).
math: Travel to school (one class) → pie or bar
Noon temperature for 14 days → line
Books read by boys and girls in Classes 6–8 → double bar

modules.title: Pose statistical questions and draw conclusions from data

chapter.title: What makes a question statistical
text: A statistical question is answered by collecting data that VARIES. 'How tall am I?' has one answer. 'How tall are the students in Class 7?' needs many measurements that differ.
math: Not statistical: What time does school start?
Statistical: What time do students in our class wake up on school days?

chapter.title: Worked: an investigation from question to conclusion
text: Question: Do students in Class 7 sleep more on weekend nights than on school nights?
math: 1. Plan: ask all 20 students in the class the hours they slept last Sunday night and last Tuesday night. — The same nights for everyone
2. Collect and record in a table. — One row per student
3. Summarise: school night total 162 h, mean 162 ÷ 20 = 8.1 h; weekend total 186 h, mean 186 ÷ 20 = 9.3 h. — Mean = total ÷ number
4. Display: a double bar graph of grouped hours. — Compares two sets
5. Conclude: these students slept about 1.2 hours more on the weekend night. — From the evidence
6. Limit: one class, one week, hours remembered by the students. — What the data cannot show

chapter.title: Conclusions the data can support
text: A conclusion must stay inside the group the data came from, and must not claim more than the data shows.
chapter.tip: A survey of your class says something about your class, not all of India. And when two things go together, that does not prove one causes the other.

strategies.title: Look for variability

screens.title: Would different people give different answers?
text: Ask: to answer this, would I need to collect answers from many people or things, and would those answers differ? If yes, it is statistical.
math: 'How many brothers and sisters do students in our class have?' → answers vary → statistical
'How many students are in our class?' → one count → not statistical

strategies.title: From question to conclusion, step by step

screens.title: Plan, collect, organise, conclude
text: 1. Make the question precise: who, what, when, which units.
2. Choose who to ask: a fair sample, not only friends.
3. Record and organise: table, then a display.
4. Conclude from the evidence, and state the limits.
math: Vague: Do people like sport?
Precise: Which sport do students in Classes 6–8 of our school most like to play?
